title: Designing a search query cache

facts.text: The service handles a user's search request that hits the cache and one that misses it, and must be highly available.
Assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, popular queries should almost always be in the cache, serving from cache needs fast lookups, and latency between machines must be low.
Cache memory is limited yet millions of queries must be cached, so the design must decide what to keep or remove and how to expire or refresh entries.
The scale is 10 million users, 10 billion queries per month and 4,000 requests per second.
The cache stores an ordered list of key (query) and value (results); an entry is a 50-byte query, 20-byte title and 200-byte snippet, 270 bytes in total.
If all 10 billion queries were unique and all were stored, the cache data would be 2.7 TB per month (270 bytes per search times 10 billion searches per month).

A memory cache such as Redis or Memcached serves popular queries, cutting read latency and sparing the Reverse Index and Document Services. Reading 1 MB sequentially takes about 250 microseconds from memory; SSD takes 4x and disk 80x longer.

The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization, converts it to boolean operations and checks the cache.
On a cache hit, the memory cache moves the entry to the front of the LRU list and returns the cached contents.
On a miss, the Query API gets ranked matching documents from the Reverse Index Service and titles and snippets from the Document Service, then caches the entry at the front of the LRU list.
Since cache capacity is limited, a least recently used (LRU) approach expires the older entries.
The cache is a doubly-linked list, with new items added at the head and items to expire removed from the tail, plus a hash table giving fast lookup of each list node.

Entries must be updated when page contents change, a page is added or removed, or page rank changes. The simplest way is a maximum time an entry may stay cached, the time to live (TTL); this approach is cache-aside.

To handle the request load and memory needed, scale the cache horizontally. Giving each machine its own cache is simple but likely gives a low hit rate, and giving each a full copy is simple but wastes memory.
Sharding the cache across all machines in the cluster is more complex but likely the best option. A hash such as machine = hash(query) picks the machine, and consistent hashing is likely wanted.

title: Doubly linked list

definition.text: A linked data structure of sequentially linked nodes, each holding a data field plus links to the previous and the next node.

facts.text: The two links allow traversal in either direction, and the direction can change mid-way. The first and last nodes (head and tail) are directly accessible, and any node can start a new traversal.
The first and last links point to a terminator, typically null or a sentinel node. With a single sentinel the list becomes circular.

Adding or removing a node changes more links than in a singly linked list, but is simpler and often more efficient, since a node already links to its predecessor and no traversal is needed to find it.
Removal needs special handling when the node is the first or last, so the list's head and tail references are updated. Deleting the only node correctly sets both to null.
